{{Short description|3d hypersurface of degree 5}}
In mathematics, a '''quintic threefold''' is a  3-dimensional hypersurface of degree 5 in 4-dimensional [[projective space]] <math>\mathbb{P}^4</math>. Non-singular quintic threefolds are [[Calabi–Yau manifold]]s.

The [[Hodge diamond]] of a non-singular quintic 3-fold is
{{Hodge diamond
|1
|0|0
|0|1|0
|1|101|101|1
|0|1|0
|0|0
|1
}}

Physicist [[Robbert Dijkgraaf]] said "One number which every algebraic geometer knows is the number 2,875 because obviously, that is the number of lines on a quintic."<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6oWLIVNI6VA  |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/6oWLIVNI6VA |archive-date=2021-12-21 |url-status=live|title=The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Quantum Physics in Modern Mathematics |author=Robbert Dijkgraaf |author-link=Robbert Dijkgraaf |publisher=Trev M |work=youtube.com |date=29 March 2015 |access-date=10 September 2015}}{{cbignore}} see 29 minutes 57 seconds</ref>

== Definition ==
A quintic threefold is a special class of [[Calabi–Yau manifold]]s defined by a degree <math>5</math> projective variety in <math>\mathbb{P}^4</math>. Many examples are constructed as [[hypersurface]]s in <math>\mathbb{P}^4</math>, or [[complete intersection]]s lying in <math>\mathbb{P}^4</math>, or as a smooth variety resolving the singularities of another variety. As a set, a Calabi-Yau manifold is<math display="block">X = \{x = [x_0:x_1:x_2:x_3:x_4] \in \mathbb{CP}^4 : p(x) = 0 \}</math>where <math>p(x)</math> is a degree <math>5</math> [[homogeneous polynomial]]. One of the most studied examples is from the polynomial<math display="block">p(x) = x_0^5 + x_1^5 + x_2^5 + x_3^5 + x_4^5</math>called a [[Diagonal form|Fermat polynomial]]. Proving that such a polynomial defines a Calabi-Yau requires some more tools, like the [[Adjunction formula]] and [[Smooth scheme|conditions for smoothness]].

=== Hypersurfaces in P<sup>4</sup> ===
Recall that a homogeneous polynomial <math>f \in \Gamma(\mathbb{P}^4,\mathcal{O}(d))</math> (where <math>\mathcal{O}(d)</math> is the Serre-twist of the [[Hyperplane bundle|hyperplane line bundle]]) defines a [[projective variety]], or [[projective scheme]], <math>X</math>, from the algebra<math display="block">\frac{k[x_0,\ldots, x_4]}{(f)}</math>where <math>k</math> is a field, such as <math>\mathbb{C}</math>. Then using the [[adjunction formula]] to compute its [[canonical bundle]], we have<math display="block">\begin{align}
\Omega_X^3 &= \omega_X \\
&= \omega_{\mathbb{P}^4}\otimes \mathcal{O}(d) \\
&\cong \mathcal{O}(-(4+1))\otimes\mathcal{O}(d) \\
&\cong \mathcal{O}(d-5)
\end{align}</math>hence in order for the variety to be Calabi-Yau, meaning it has a trivial canonical bundle, its degree must be <math>5</math>. It is then a Calabi-Yau manifold if in addition this variety is [[Smooth variety|smooth]]. This can be checked by looking at the zeros of the polynomials<math display="block">\partial_0f,\ldots, \partial_4f</math>and making sure the set<math display="block">\{ x = [x_0:\cdots:x_4] | f(x) = \partial_0f(x) = \cdots = \partial_4f(x) = 0 \}</math>is empty.

== Examples ==

=== Fermat Quintic ===
One of the easiest examples to check of a Calabi-Yau manifold is given by the [[Fermat quintic threefold]], which is defined by the vanishing locus of the polynomial<math display="block">f = x_0^5 + x_1^5 + x_2^5 + x_3^5 + x_4^5</math>Computing the partial derivatives of <math>f</math> gives the four polynomials<math display="block">\begin{align}
\partial_0f = 5x_0^4\\
\partial_1f = 5x_1^4 \\
\partial_2f = 5x_2^4 \\
\partial_3f = 5x_3^4 \\
\partial_4f = 5x_4^4 \\
\end{align}</math>Since the only points where they vanish is given by the coordinate axes in <math>\mathbb{P}^4</math>, the vanishing locus is empty since <math>[0:0:0:0:0]</math> is not a point in <math>\mathbb{P}^4</math>.

==== As a Hodge Conjecture testbed ====
Another application of the quintic threefold is in the study of the [[infinitesimal]] generalized [[Hodge conjecture]] where this difficult problem can be solved in this case.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Albano|first1=Alberto|last2=Katz|first2=Sheldon|date=1991|title=Lines on the Fermat quintic threefold and the infinitesimal generalized Hodge conjecture|url=https://www.ams.org/tran/1991-324-01/S0002-9947-1991-1024767-6/|journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society|language=en|volume=324|issue=1|pages=353–368|doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1991-1024767-6|issn=0002-9947|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In fact, all of the lines on this hypersurface can be found explicitly.

=== Dwork family of quintic three-folds ===
Another popular class of examples of quintic three-folds, studied in many contexts, is the [[Dwork family]]. One popular study of such a family is from Candelas, De La Ossa, Green, and Parkes,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Candelas|first1=Philip|last2=De La Ossa|first2=Xenia C.|last3=Green|first3=Paul S.|last4=Parkes|first4=Linda|date=1991-07-29|title=A pair of Calabi-Yau manifolds as an exactly soluble superconformal theory|url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0550-3213%2891%2990292-6|journal=Nuclear Physics B|language=en|volume=359|issue=1|pages=21–74|doi=10.1016/0550-3213(91)90292-6|bibcode=1991NuPhB.359...21C|issn=0550-3213|url-access=subscription}}</ref> when they discovered [[Mirror symmetry (string theory)|mirror symmetry]]. This is given by the family<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Gross|first1=Mark|author-link=Mark Gross (mathematician)|url=https://www.springer.com/gp/book/9783540440598|title=Calabi-Yau Manifolds and Related Geometries: Lectures at a Summer School in Nordfjordeid, Norway, June 2001|last2=Huybrechts|first2=Daniel|author-link2=Daniel Huybrechts|last3=Joyce|first3=Dominic|author-link3=Dominic Joyce|date=2003|publisher=Springer-Verlag|isbn=978-3-540-44059-8|editor-last=Ellingsrud|editor-first=Geir|series=Universitext|location=Berlin Heidelberg|pages=123–125|language=en|editor-last2=Olson|editor-first2=Loren|editor-last3=Ranestad|editor-first3=Kristian|editor-last4=Stromme|editor-first4=Stein A.}}</ref> <sup>pages 123-125</sup><math display="block">f_\psi = x_0^5 + x_1^5 + x_2^5 + x_3^5 + x_4^5 - 5\psi x_0x_1x_2x_3x_4</math>where <math>\psi</math> is a single parameter not equal to a 5-th [[root of unity]]. The smoothness of the quintic for these parameters can be found by computing the partial derivates of <math>f_\psi</math> and evaluating their zeros. The partial derivatives are given by<math display="block">\begin{align}
\partial_0f_\psi = 5x_0^4 - 5\psi x_1x_2x_3x_4 \\
\partial_1f_\psi = 5x_1^4 - 5\psi x_0x_2x_3x_4 \\
\partial_2f_\psi = 5x_2^4 - 5\psi x_0x_1x_3x_4 \\
\partial_3f_\psi = 5x_3^4 - 5\psi x_0x_1x_2x_4\\
\partial_4f_\psi = 5x_4^4 - 5\psi x_0x_1x_2x_3\\
\end{align}</math>At a point where the partial derivatives are all zero, this gives the relation <math>x_i^5 = \psi x_0x_1x_2x_3x_4</math>. For example, in <math>\partial_0f_\psi</math> we get<math display="block">\begin{align}
5x_0^4 &= 5\psi x_1x_2x_3x_4 \\
x_0^4 &= \psi x_1x_2x_3x_4 \\
x_0^5 &= \psi x_0x_1x_2x_3x_4
\end{align}</math>by dividing out the <math>5</math> and multiplying each side by <math>x_0</math>. From multiplying these families of equations <math>x_i^5 = \psi x_0x_1x_2x_3x_4</math> together we have the relation<math display="block">\prod x_i^5 = \psi^5 \prod x_i^5</math>showing a solution is either given by an <math>x_i = 0</math> or <math>\psi^5 = 1</math>. But in the first case, these give a smooth sublocus since the varying term in <math>f_\psi</math> vanishes, so a singular point must lie in <math>\psi^5 = 1</math>. Given such a <math>\psi</math>, the singular points are then of the form<math display="block">[\mu_5^{a_0}:\cdots:\mu_5^{a_4}]</math> such that <math display="block">\mu_5^{\sum a_i}=\psi^{-1}</math>where <math>\mu_5 = e^{2 \pi i / 5}</math>. For example, the point<math display="block">[\mu_5^4:\mu_5^{-1}:\mu_5^{-1}:\mu_5^{-1}:\mu_5^{-1}]</math>is a solution of both <math>f_1</math> and its partial derivatives since <math>(\mu_5^i)^5 = (\mu_5^5)^i = 1^i = 1</math>, and <math>\psi = 1</math>.

== Curves on a quintic threefold ==
The number of rational curves of degree <math>1</math> can be computed explicitly using [[Schubert calculus]]. Let <math>T^*</math> be the rank <math>2</math> [[vector bundle]] on the [[Grassmannian]] <math>G(2,5)</math> of <math>2</math>-planes in some rank <math>5</math> [[vector space]]. Projectivizing <math>G(2,5)</math> to <math>\mathbb{G}(1,4)</math> gives the projective Grassmannian of degree <math>1</math> lines in <math>\mathbb{P}^4</math> and <math>T^*</math> [[Descent theory|descends]] to a vector bundle on this projective Grassmannian. Its total [[Chern class]] is<math display="block">c(T^*) = 1 + \sigma_1 + \sigma_{1,1}</math>in the [[Chow ring]] <math>A^\bullet(\mathbb{G}(1,4))</math>. Now, a section <math>l \in \Gamma(\mathbb{G}(1,4),T^*)</math> of the bundle corresponds to a linear homogeneous polynomial, <math>\tilde{l} \in \Gamma(\mathbb{P}^4,\mathcal{O}(1))</math>, so a section of <math>\text{Sym}^5(T^*)</math> corresponds to a quintic polynomial, a section of <math>\Gamma(\mathbb{P}^4,\mathcal{O}(5))</math>. Then, in order to calculate the number of lines on a generic quintic threefold, it suffices to compute the integral<ref>{{Cite book|last=Katz|first=Sheldon|title=Enumerative Geometry and String Theory|pages=108}}</ref><math display="block">\int_{\mathbb{G}(1,4)} c(\text{Sym}^5(T^*)) = 2875</math>This can be done by using the [[splitting principle]]. Since<math display="block">\begin{align}
c(T^*) &= (1+\alpha)(1+\beta) \\
&= 1 + (\alpha + \beta) + \alpha\beta
\end{align}</math>and for a dimension <math>2</math> vector space, <math>V = V_1\oplus V_2</math>,<math display="block">\text{Sym}^5(V) = \bigoplus_{i=0}^5 (V_1^{\otimes 5-i}\otimes V_2^{\otimes i})</math>so the total Chern class of <math>\text{Sym}^5(T^*)</math> is given by the product<math display="block">c(\text{Sym}^5(T^*)) = \prod_{i=0}^5 (1 + (5-i)\alpha  + i\beta)</math>Then, the [[Euler class]], or the top class is<math display="block">5\alpha(4\alpha + \beta)(3\alpha + 2\beta)(2\alpha + 3\beta)(\alpha + 4\beta)5\beta</math>expanding this out in terms of the original Chern classes gives<math display="block">\begin{align}
c_6(\text{Sym}^5(T^*)) &= 25\sigma_{1,1}(4\sigma_1^2 + 9\sigma_{1,1})(6\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_{1,1}) \\
&= (100 \sigma_{3,1} + 100\sigma_{2,2} + 225\sigma_{2,2})(6\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_{1,1}) \\
&= (100 \sigma_{3,1} + 325\sigma_{2,2})(6\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_{1,1})\\
&= 600 \sigma_{3,3} + 2275 \sigma_{3,3}\\
&= 2875 \sigma_{3,3}
\end{align}</math>using relations implied by [[Pieri's formula]], including <math>\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2 + \sigma_{1,1}</math>, <math>\sigma_{1,1}\cdot \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_{3,1} + \sigma_{2,2}</math>, <math>\sigma_{1,1}^2 = \sigma_{2,2}</math>.

===Rational curves===
{{harvs|txt|last=Clemens | first=Herbert | authorlink=Herbert Clemens | year=1984}} conjectured that the number of rational curves of a given degree on a generic quintic threefold is finite. (Some smooth but non-generic quintic threefolds have infinite families of lines on them.) This was verified for degrees up to 7 by {{harvs|txt| last=Katz | first=Sheldon |authorlink=Sheldon Katz|year=1986}} who also calculated the number 609250 of degree 2 rational curves. 
Brian Greene and Ronen Plesser (1989) proposed a construction for a mirror manifold of quintic threefolds.
{{harvs|txt| last1=Candelas | first1=Philip | author1-link=Philip Candelas | last2=de la Ossa | authorlink2=Xenia de la Ossa | first2=Xenia C. | last3=Green | first3=Paul S. | last4=Parkes | first4=Linda | title=A pair of Calabi-Yau manifolds as an exactly soluble superconformal theory | doi=10.1016/0550-3213(91)90292-6  | mr=1115626  | year=1991 | journal=Nuclear Physics B | volume=359 | issue=1 | pages=21–74}}
conjectured a general formula for the virtual number of rational curves of any degree. The formula  was independently verified by {{harvtxt|Givental|1996}} and {{harvs | txt | last1=Lian | first1=B. | last2=Liu | first2=K. | author2-link=Kefeng Liu | last3=Yau | first3=S.-T. | author3-link=Shing-Tung Yau | title=Mirror Principle I | mr=1621573  | year=1997 | journal=Asian J. Math. | volume=1 | issue=4 | pages=729-763}}. The fact that the virtual number equals the actual number relies on confirmation of Clemens' conjecture, currently known for degree at most 11 {{harvtxt|Cotterill|2012}}.
The number of rational curves of various degrees on a generic quintic threefold is given by 
:2875, 609250, 317206375, 242467530000, ...{{OEIS|A076912}}.
Since the generic quintic threefold is a Calabi–Yau threefold and the [[moduli space]] of rational curves of a given degree is a discrete, [[finite set]] (hence compact), these have well-defined [[Donaldson–Thomas invariant]]s (the "virtual number of points"); at least for degree 1 and 2, these agree with the actual number of points.
